מנצח is rendered 'choirmaster' (STEPBible) in the glosses but 'the Leader' in the literal layer: the meaning of the title is disputed (director, overseer, or a liturgical term).

agent_notes: Commentary on סתרו: the Hebrew ordering is ambiguous between 'he made darkness his covering, around him his canopy' and 'he made darkness his covering around him, his canopy …'. The accents (zaqef on סתרו-ס֗ and etnachta on סכתו) support the second grouping only partly; I kept the literal rendering close to the Hebrew order so both readings survive.

The packet gave no dramatic text for PS.18.12, so the voice of this window is set here: slow, storm-heavy, in the present-tense hush of a theophany remembered. Check it against the voice of PS.18.1-12 when that window is merged.

The Masoretic text has עָבָיו עָבְרוּ with a plural verb after a plural noun; the construction is plain. I read עָבְרוּ as 'passed on / swept on', the sense of YLT and Rashi, not 'passed away'. 'Hail and coals of fire' is read as the content of what the clouds carried (Metzudat David), not as a separate subject.

רָב is glossed 'he shot' on the reading, defended by Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Radak, that it is a perfect of רבב (cf. Gen 49:23 וְרֹבּוּ). KJV, ASV and YLT take בְרָקִים רָב as 'lightnings many', which is also possible if רב is the adjective; the verb reading gives the arrow parallel.

history.note: [consider] Drop 'like chaff', or replace it with an image that stays with the arrows. (PS.18.15: "וַיִּשְׁלַח חִצָּיו וַיְפִיצֵם".)

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses אַפֶּךָ 'nostrils' while the lemma אַף also means anger; both senses are alive. I keep 'nostrils' in the literal layer and bring out 'anger' in the commentary.

The imperfect verbs (יִשְׁלַח, יִקָּחֵנִי, יַמְשֵׁנִי, יַצִּילֵנִי, and so on) run on through v.20 after the wayyiqtols of vv.14-16. The literal layer follows the Hebrew forms with 'he sends'; the dramatic layer narrates them in the past, as KJV does, since the whole is a remembered rescue. The tenses are a real choice, not a certainty.

history.note: [consider] Present the Moses echo as a possible resonance, not as what a listener would hear, and correct the verse count. (Rashi on PS.18.17: "לשון הוצאה, כמו כי מן המים משיתהו".)

agent_notes: Revised per the reviewer request: the commentary and the note on אֹיְבִי עָז now say that Radak reads the singular 'strong enemy' as Goliath or Ishbi-benob (Radak: 'על גלית או ישבי בנב'; Ishbi-benob is in 2 Sam 21:16), and no longer mention the people of Nob. Meiri reads the same singular as Saul; I give both without choosing.

STEPBible glosses יַצִּילֵנִי as past 'he rescued me'. The form is imperfect, and the psalm's frame (vv. 4-17) narrates a completed rescue, so I gloss it 'he rescues me' in the literal layer and render the dramatic layer in the past. The KJV and ASV also use 'delivered'; YLT's present is the closest to the Hebrew form.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses יְקַדְּמוּנִי 'they confronted me'. I keep that but note the idea 'they came to meet me ahead of time' (Rashi). KJV 'prevented' is Elizabethan for 'came before'.

ארחמך: Qal of רחם is otherwise unattested in this sense (the Qal elsewhere is not found; Piel means 'have compassion'). I follow Rashi, Radak and the Targum ('I love you'); Ibn Ezra offers 'I seek mercy from you'. The parallel in 2 Sam 22 lacks this line.
The word-count in the packet's morphology gives כִּי a translit 'kiSha', a packet artifact; the token is plain כִּי.

Meiri reads מֵעֲוֹנִי as 'from my (particular) iniquity', the one a man is prone to; I cite him but flag it as one reading. The classical 'my iniquity' need not be a confession of sin: the claim is of habitual self-guarding.

The packet shows no preceding verse text for this window, so the dramatic voice starts fresh here and is carried forward verse by verse. The verb vayyashev is a wayyiqtol: 'returned/repaid'. With the preceding verses (vv. 21-24) it reads as a summary of what has happened; I kept the past tense, as the five English versions do not agree (YLT present, KJV/ASV perfect).

Revised per the reviewer request: the sentence about meeting people with less or more than they bring is cut from the dramatic layer, which now holds only the two clauses of the Hebrew. The BDB source is replaced by Ibn Ezra on 18:26 and Radak on 18:26, both in the packet. The line in the director's commentary that mentions 'more than deserved' is Radak's, and it is cited as his.

The verse is general, the first of the maxims in vv. 26-27 (Radak and Metzudat David take it as God's usual way of acting). The Targum applies it to Abraham and Isaac; Rashi adds the third father with גבר as Jacob. I cite those two without adopting them.

agent_notes: naVar (H1305, Niphal participle of brr) is glossed 'one who is purified/pure' and titbaRar as a Hithpael of the same root. STEPBible lemmatises both under H1305 (barar); Rashi glosses naVar as 'faithful' (ne'eman), which I do not follow. Rendering the Hithpael as 'show yourself pure' follows the pattern of the preceding verse.

titpaTal (Hithpael of ptl, 'twist') has the same root as Jacob's wrestling in Gen 30:8 (naftulei) and the 'twisted' generation of Deut 32:5 (ptltl); YLT 'a wrestler' and Webster 'contend' push toward the wrestling sense, while KJV/ASV 'froward' only gives the moral sense. I kept 'twisted' in the literal layer and let the dramatic layer carry the matching of crookedness with crookedness.

STEPBible tags אלי with deity.yhwh and glosses 'God my'; kept. The five English versions split on צורי: KJV and Webster 'my strength' (harmonized with v.2 חזקי), while YLT, ASV and BBE keep 'rock'. The Hebrew repeats צור, so 'rock' is right.

Revision: the crag of the Divisions is now attributed in both places the packet has it. Rashi on סלעי names it and cites 1 Sam 23:26 (Saul's men closing round David); Radak on 18:5 names it with the reference 1 Sam 23:28, where the place is named. The reference is no longer given as Rashi's alone.

agent_notes: The STEPBible gloss for 'aRutz is 'I run' with gedud as object ('a marauding band'); the verb is read by Radak and Meiri as possibly from rtz (to crush, 'I shatter a band'). I kept the plain 'run' reading with a note on the alternative. The parallel in 2 Sam 22:30 has the same consonants.
I did not quote the midrashic stories (Joab and the cypress, Yalkut/Midrash Tehillim) as fact about the verse; Rashi and Radak report them and the commentary mentions them only as a later reading.

Addressed the request: the commentary now says the KJV renders both mibbal'adei and zulati with 'save' and so flattens the variation. Webster does the same; BBE uses 'but' for both; ASV and YLT vary ('save'/'besides'), so the Hebrew's two different words are carried only in those. STEPBible glosses word 3 '[is] God' and word 7 '[is] a rock'; I kept 'is' out of the glosses as supplied, and bracketed it in the literal.

agent_notes: venichaTah is a rare and disputed form: Rashi derives it from nacham/ncht (to tread a bow, pull it), Ibn Ezra offers nun as root letter or a Niphal; Metzudat Zion links it to 'break'. KJV 'broken' follows the sense 'bring down'. I chose 'is bent down / pressed down' (a bow drawn). STEPBible gloss 'it will stretch' is corrected to 'and [a bow] is bent'. Singular verb with a plural noun 'arms' is also noted: the bow is the subject, 'my arms' the instrument.

Addressed the request: the commentary no longer calls the direct address new. It describes the return to 'you' after the third-person verses 31-35 (the 'you' last heard at vv. 26-28). 'anvatkha is a hard word: the versions split (KJV 'gentleness', YLT 'lowliness', BBE 'mercy'); I kept 'humility' in the literal layer and left the commentary's reading of it as stooping, the sense Radak and Metzudat David give. I did not rely on the parallel text in 2 Samuel 22 for the choice.

agent_notes: קַרְסֻלָּי is a dual noun 'my ankles'. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri read it as 'legs/knees' via the Targum's רכוּבְתִּי and Lev 11:21 (כרעים); I keep 'ankles', which is the plain sense and what YLT has, and mention the tradition in the commentary.

history.note: [consider] Rephrase: the Targum uses קרסולין for כרעים ('legs') in Lev 11:21, so Radak and others take קרסלי as legs or knees. (Radak on PS.18.37: "קרסלי: כרעי, כתרגום אשר לו כרעים (ויקרא יא כא): דיליה קרסולין".)

agent_notes: The verbs in vv. 38-48 are imperfects (yiqtol) with a few wayyiqtols. KJV and Webster render them as completed ('I have pursued'), ASV as future ('I will pursue'), YLT and BBE as present. I render the literal layer as a present or habitual and the dramatic layer as a sweeping narrative in the present, since the psalm is a king's recital of victory that the text itself leaves open in tense.

Addressed the request: the commentary now points back to the previous verse's 'not able to rise' (v. 39), with qamai ('those who rose') answering the verb qum there. The packet's gloss of word 5 '[those who] rose against me' is kept, as a participle.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses עֹרֶף as 'neck'. The idiom 'to give the neck' means to make enemies turn their backs in flight; Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David all say so. Literal layer keeps 'neck', the commentary gives the idiom.

עַל־יְהוָה is 'to YHWH' (עַל for אֶל); Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri say so, citing 1 Sam 1:10. Rashi and Metzudat David think the first cry is to their own gods or to human helpers; the Hebrew does not say, so the dramatic layer follows the plain text, which has the enemies finally crying to YHWH.

אֲרִיקֵם: STEPBible 'I poured out them' (root ריק, hiphil). Radak argues a root רקק (make like spittle/mire), Meiri a doubled root with yod for the dagesh. I keep 'pour out / empty out'; the mud-like image is the same either way. Rashi cites Gen 42:35 and Jer 48:11 for the sense of pouring.

Radak notes that 2 Sam 22:44 reads 'מֵרִיבֵי עַמִּי' (my people). In Psalm 18 the word is עָם without the suffix, so the 'strivings of a people' is ambiguous: Israel's own factions (Saul, Absalom, Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak) or foreign nations (Meiri, Metzudat David). The literal layer keeps 'a people'; the dramatic layer stays with the broader 'strife of a people'.

יְכַחֲשׁוּ (piel of כחשׁ) is 'to lie, to feign, to cringe'. STEPBible 'cringe'; YLT 'feign obedience'; BBE 'with false hearts'; Rashi says 'out of fear'. I gloss it 'they feign / cringe' and render the literal layer 'they lie to me', because the Hebrew keeps the word 'lie' and the English versions split.

וְיַחְרְגוּ: the Qere/Ketiv-free form here is from חרג, a hapax; Targum and Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri say 'tremble' (from Deut 32:25 חרגת מותא). Rashi cites Menahem's 'loosening of the girdle' and Dunash's 'limp like shackled men'; Malbim 'come lame from the journey'. I take 'come trembling', which is also what STEPBible and ASV do, and cite the alternatives. 2 Sam 22:46 has ויחגרו from חגר, which I flag but do not use.

יִבֹּלוּ: STEPBible gives 'they wither' (נבל, to fade). Rashi first reads it as 'grow weary' via Ex 18:18 (נָבֹל תִּבֹּל), then cites Menahem; Metzudat David 'be in pain'. I keep 'wither' and flag the alternative.

agent_notes: וַיַּדְבֵּר: STEPBible 'subdue'. Rashi first 'kill' (from דבר, plague), then 'lead' (cf. Ex 3:1, Targum וּדְבַר); Radak and Meiri 'lead them out of their places and put them under me'; Metzudat David 'made me their leader'. The Hebrew is the hiphil of דבר, 'drive/lead', as in Ps 47:4; I give 'he drives peoples under me' in the literal layer and flag the 'subdue' tradition in the commentary.

mefaleTi is a participle with a suffix ('my deliverer / the one delivering me'); the five English versions split between present ('delivereth') and perfect. I kept the participle in the literal layer and let the dramatic layer carry the sense of ongoing rescue. The two later verbs are imperfects; STEPBible's perfect 'have exalted/rescued' is corrected to a habitual-present reading.

Who 'the man of violence' is: Ibn Ezra offers a Philistine king or Saul; Radak and Meiri say Saul. The text does not name him, so the dramatic layer keeps him unnamed. The Targum's Gog is not followed.
